scenes.title: HIPAA Compliance Training
scenes.subtitle: Protecting patient privacy is everyone's job
scenes.say: Welcome to hippa compliance training. If you work with patient information, in any role, the law requires you to protect it. In the next few minutes, we'll cover what hippa is, what counts as protected health information, the rules you need to follow, and what to do when something goes wrong. You'll also test yourself with three real world scenarios. This video is general training. Always follow your own organization's policies.

scenes.title: What is HIPAA?
items: A U.S. federal law
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996
Hippa is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. A United States federal law, passed in nineteen ninety six.
It protects patient health information
National standards for privacy, security, and patient rights
It sets national standards for protecting patient health information, and it gives patients rights over their own records.
It applies to covered entities
Providers, health plans, and clearinghouses
It applies to covered entities. That means health care providers, health plans, and health care clearing houses.
And to business associates
Vendors that handle patient data: billing, IT, cloud
And it applies to their business associates. Those are vendors that handle patient information on their behalf, such as billing companies, I.T. providers, and cloud services.

scenes.title: Protected Health Information
scenes.say: Next, protected health information, or P H I.
items: Health information that identifies a person
About their health, their care, or payment for care
P H I is any information about a person's health, their care, or payment for that care, that can be linked to that individual.
Any form counts
Paper, electronic, or spoken
It counts in any form. On paper, in a computer system, or spoken out loud.
18 types of identifiers
Names, dates, addresses, phone numbers, SSNs, photos…
Hippa lists eighteen types of identifiers. They include names, dates, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, social security numbers, medical record numbers, and full face photos.
When in doubt, treat it as PHI
Even confirming someone is a patient can be a disclosure
When in doubt, treat it as P H I. Even confirming that someone is a patient can be a disclosure.

scenes.title: The Privacy Rule
scenes.say: The privacy rule controls how P H I may be used and shared.
items: Treatment, payment, and operations
Permitted without the patient's written authorization
You may use and share P H I for treatment, payment, and health care operations, without the patient's written authorization.
Most other uses need authorization
Such as marketing — apart from specific legal exceptions
Most other uses, such as marketing, need the patient's written authorization, apart from specific exceptions set out in the law, like public health reporting.
Minimum necessary
Use, share, and access only what your job requires
Follow the minimum necessary standard. Use, share, and access only the information you need to do your job.
Patients have rights
To see, copy, and correct their records
And remember, patients have rights. They can see and get copies of their records, ask for corrections, and ask who their information was shared with.

scenes.title: What would you do?
scenes.question: A well-known local figure is admitted to your facility. You're not involved in their care, but you're curious about what happened.
options: Take a quick look at the chart — no one will know
Ask a coworker who is treating them
Don't look and don't ask — you have no job-related need
scenes.explain: No job-related need means no access. Record access is logged and audited.
scenes.say: Time to test yourself. Scenario one. A well known local figure is admitted to your facility. You're not involved in their care, but you're curious about what happened. What would you do? A. Take a quick look at the chart. No one will know. B. Ask a co-worker who is treating them. Or C. Don't look, and don't ask. You have no job related need.
scenes.answer_say: The answer is C. Looking at a record without a job related reason is a violation, even if you never tell anyone. Asking a co-worker is, too. Access to records is logged and audited, and snooping is one of the most common reasons people are disciplined, or lose their jobs.

scenes.title: The Security Rule
scenes.say: The security rule protects electronic P H I, with three kinds of safeguards.
items: Administrative safeguards
Risk analysis, policies, training, access management
Administrative safeguards. Risk analysis, written policies, workforce training, and managing who has access.
Physical safeguards
Locked areas, screen privacy, secure disposal
Physical safeguards. Locked areas, screens turned away from public view, and secure disposal of devices and paper.
Technical safeguards
Unique logins, encryption, audit logs, automatic logoff
Technical safeguards. Unique log-ins, encryption, audit logs, and automatic log off.
Your part, every day
Never share a login · Lock your screen · Approved tools only
And your part, every day. Never share your log-in. Lock your screen when you step away. And only use approved systems to store, or send, P H I.

scenes.title: What would you do?
scenes.question: A doctor asks you to text a photo of a patient's lab result to their personal cell phone, to save time.
options: Text it — it's for patient care
Send it from your personal email instead
Use the approved secure messaging system
scenes.explain: Good reason, wrong method. Ordinary texts and personal email aren't secure.
scenes.say: Scenario two. A doctor asks you to text a photo of a patient's lab result to their personal cell phone, to save time. What would you do? A. Text it. It's for patient care. B. Send it from your personal email instead. Or C. Use the approved secure messaging system.
scenes.answer_say: The answer is C. The reason is good, but the method isn't. Ordinary text messages and personal email aren't secure, and they leave patient information sitting on personal devices. Always use the secure tools your organization has approved.

scenes.title: Common mistakes to avoid
scenes.say: Most violations aren't malicious. They're everyday mistakes. Here are the common ones.
items: Talking where others can hear
Hallways, elevators, and waiting areas
Talking about patients where others can hear. In hallways, elevators, and waiting areas.
Sending to the wrong person
Double-check every email, fax, and mailing
Sending information to the wrong person. Double check every email address, fax number, and mailing.
Posting on social media
No patient details or photos — even without a name
Posting on social media. Never share patient details or photos, even without a name.
Lost or stolen devices
Unencrypted laptops, phones, and USB drives
Lost or stolen devices. One unencrypted laptop, phone, or U S B drive can expose thousands of records.
Careless disposal
Shred paper records — never the regular trash
And careless disposal. Shred paper records. Never put them in the regular trash.

scenes.title: Breaches and reporting
items: What is a breach?
An impermissible use or disclosure that compromises PHI
A breach is an impermissible use or disclosure of P H I, that compromises its security or privacy.
Report it internally right away
To your privacy officer or security officer
If you suspect one, report it right away, to your privacy officer or security officer. Don't try to investigate, or fix it, on your own.
The clock is ticking
Notify individuals within 60 days · 500+ people: HHS and media too

The clock starts when the breach is discovered. The organization must notify affected individuals without unreasonable delay, and no later than sixty days. Breaches affecting five hundred or more people must also be reported to the Department of Health and Human Services, and to the media.
Penalties are serious
Fines, job loss, and even criminal charges
And the penalties are serious. Organizations can face large fines. Individuals can lose their jobs, and for deliberate misuse, face criminal charges.

scenes.title: What would you do?
scenes.question: You just emailed a patient's records to the wrong person — a stranger with a similar email address.
options: Try to recall the email and say nothing
Ask the stranger to delete it, then move on
Report it to your privacy officer immediately
scenes.explain: Report fast. Hiding a mistake turns a small problem into a serious one.
scenes.say: Scenario three. You just emailed a patient's records to the wrong person. A stranger, with a similar email address. What would you do? A. Try to recall the email, and say nothing. B. Ask the stranger to delete it, then move on. Or C. Report it to your privacy officer immediately.
scenes.answer_say: The answer is C. Mistakes happen. What matters is how fast you report them. Your privacy officer will decide what needs to be done, and whether anyone must be notified. Hiding a mistake turns a small problem into a serious one.

scenes.title: Four habits that protect patients
scenes.say: So, here's what to remember. Four habits.
items: Limit
Access only what your job requires
Limit. Access only what your job requires.
Protect
Lock screens, use approved tools, shred paper
Protect. Lock your screen, use approved tools, and shred paper.
Verify
Confirm who you're talking to before you share
Verify. Confirm who you're talking to, before you share anything.
Report
Right away, to your privacy or security officer
And report. Right away, to your privacy or security officer. Behind every record is a real person, who is trusting you with it. Thanks for watching.
